column1: Food for Thought: How Can Machine Learning Help Better Understand Food Affordability?

The thesis titled Food for thought: How can machine learning help better predict and understand changes in food prices? by Kristina L. Kupferschmidt and colleagues addresses the challenge of understanding fluctuations in food affordability in Canada. The study is part of the efforts of Canada's Food Price Report (CFPR)  an annual publication that forecasts food inflation for the upcoming year. The CFPR is a collaborative project involving several Canadian universities  including Dalhousie University  the University of British Columbia  the University of Saskatchewan  and the University of Guelph/Vector Institute. The University of Guelph/Vector Institute team has previously utilized machine learning (ML) in their forecasting efforts  and the most recent reports (2024–2025) have incorporated a human-in-the-loop approach. For the 2025 report  the focus was expanded to evaluate various data-centric approaches to improve forecast accuracy.

The study evaluates different forecasting models' performance in estimating food price fluctuations and examines the sensitivity of models that curate time series data representing key factors in food pricing. Food affordability is a significant issue in Canada  with many Canadians struggling with recent cost of living increases. Food prices are influenced by various factors  including climate events  supply chain disruptions  policy changes  and geopolitical factors. In 2023  affordability concerns were heightened due to high inflation  which led to increased costs in food  housing  energy  and other expenditures. Although researchers have attempted to quantify the impacts of specific factors on food prices  these factors are not independent  and interactions between multiple regressors must be considered.

The CFPR has been published for 14 years and provides expectations of annual food expenditures for average Canadians. The 2025 CFPR was produced through a Canada-wide collaboration between Dalhousie University  the University of Guelph/Vector Institute  the University of British Columbia  and the University of Saskatchewan. The CFPR has two main objectives: to help Canadians better understand and create budgets for necessary food purchases and to provide policymakers with an estimate of food price inflation. Each autumn  the CFPR predicts the percentage change for nine food categories in the Consumer Price Index (CPI) from Statistics Canada for the upcoming year. The 2025 CFPR is scheduled for release on December 5  2024.

The CFPR employs a hybrid approach  combining judgmental forecasts with statistical and ML-based approaches. Teams at the associated universities work together to implement and present different forecasting approaches. These forecasts are then combined by a diverse team of experts in agriculture  management  economics  and computer science to produce a single predicted range for each CPI food category. The 2025 forecasts by the University of Guelph/Vector Institute team focused on a data-centric approach guided by human-centered design practices. This technical report complements Canada's Food Price Report by providing more details about the team's forecasting approach.

In the early stages of problem definition  domain experts were consulted to identify important factors driving food prices and provide suggestions on data sources and incorporation methods. These suggestions were used to complete an extensive web scraping exercise  selecting and pre-processing regressor time series reflecting expert-identified factors. A sensitivity analysis was conducted to understand the impacts of data curation using methods such as thematic grouping of regressors and applying large language models (LLMs) to curate bespoke sets of regressors for specific tasks.

The primary aim of the work contributing to the 2025 CFPR was to produce high-quality forecasts while minimizing error over selected test periods. Several additional research questions emerged  with objectives including adapting an existing human-centric forecasting framework to use a combination of human and machine experts to maximize forecasting performance  exploring methods for incorporating additional context into time-series forecasting to improve accuracy  investigating whether intrinsic characteristics of time-series data influence the effectiveness of high-capacity ML models  and comparing different model and data curation methods included in the forecasting experiments conducted for the 2025 CFPR.

The study also reviews related works  highlighting the gradual advancements in ML-based forecasting and the opportunities to improve alignment in delivering these predictions. Human-centered frameworks  such as DelphAI  facilitate expert engagement throughout the development pipeline to guide decisions to improve forecasting accuracy and usefulness. The study explores incorporating context into forecasting  noting the rapid adoption of foundation models in various domains and the limited contextual information provided to time-series forecasting models. The study aims to address these challenges by incorporating additional context and improving the alignment of ML-based forecasting with user needs.
